title: Delivering Bad News & Declining Proposals
titleEs: Dar malas noticias y rechazar propuestas
intro: The full-scale search test has gone badly, three weeks before go-live. Across the module, Ryan's team softens unwelcome facts without hiding them, turns down a generous offer from Helen without hurting the relationship, explains the limits of time, budget and scope, builds counter-proposals instead of rival plans and, finally, tells Helen, the key client, that the full search will not make the launch. The grammar at the center is hedging (modals, *seem / appear to*, downtoners) and a first look at **mixed conditionals** (*If we had tested earlier, we would be in a better position now*), which you will study in depth in B2.2. The pronunciation focus is weak forms: the small words (*can, was, for, but, had, than, could, or, as, her, from*) that native speakers reduce to a schwa.
canDo: Soften unwelcome facts with hedges and downtoners, and keep facts and commitments firm.
Decline an offer in five moves and keep the door open.
Explain time, budget and scope constraints neutrally, linking a past decision to the present with a mixed conditional.
Offer alternatives and build counter-proposals on the other person's plan.
Break bad news to a key client: warning, news, reason, ownership and plan.

focus.grammar: Hedging: may / might / could, seem / appear to, it looks as if, downtoners (slightly, a bit, somewhat), not + positive word · would for imagined acceptance and rejected alternatives · what if / would it help if + past · provided / as long as + present · preview of mixed conditionals (if + past perfect, would + bare infinitive + now)
focus.lexis: I'm afraid, not quite what we'd hoped, it looks as if, as far as we can tell, we'll have to pass, not in a position to, at this stage, leave the door open, be up against, the budget doesn't stretch to, out of scope, a change request, one option would be to, a fallback, a phased approach, as we discussed, in the meantime, go live
focus.afh: weak forms of function words: can /kən/ vs can't /kænt/, was /wəz/, some /səm/, for /fə(r)/, but /bət/, to /tə/ (strong /tuː/ at the end), 'd = had, than /ðən/, and /ənd/, could /kəd/, or /ə(r)/, as /əz/, her /ə(r)/, from /frəm/
